xray.one_line: Atlassian's AI layer, Rovo, whose agents search, write and act across Jira, Confluence and connected apps, on a user's account or their own.
xray.what_it_does: Rovo is Atlassian's AI offering for finding answers, automating tasks and making decisions with an organisation's connected context; it is powered by the Teamwork Graph, a data layer that maps relationships across people, apps, projects, code, decisions and assets. Rovo agents are configurable AI teammates that any team member can call on or create, in Chat, in automation flows, while editing in Jira and Confluence, and in Studio; with permission they organise, create or edit Jira work items and Confluence pages, and with connected tools they act in third-party apps. Rovo is available to customers on Standard, Premium and Enterprise Cloud plans, and AI is activated automatically on those plans unless an organisation admin deactivates it. [s3, s26, s2, s4, s1]

situations.title: Aug 2026: a hidden prompt in an upload sends out Jira data
reach: The Jira tickets the signed-in user can access
The Confluence documents the signed-in user can access
Data the user can reach through connectors; researchers name SharePoint and Outlook
Rovo's URL-retrieval tool, which opened a URL the agent had built itself; the organisation's web search setting did not remove it
A file the user uploaded into the chat, read in the same context as the user's request
Markdown images rendered from model output, a second outbound route PromptArmor flagged but did not demonstrate end to end
asked_our_example: Organise the user's Jira tickets, reading Jira and Confluence as needed
No data leaves the Atlassian tenant unless the user chooses to send it
As configured in the proof of concept: the organisation-wide 'Enable web search' setting for Rovo switched off
gap: Text hidden in an uploaded file was acted on as instructions alongside the user's request, and nothing checked whether a URL the agent opened was one it had composed itself.
The web search toggle the organisation relied on did not remove the URL-opening capability, so the setting did not bound outbound requests.
Everything the user could read, including connector data, sat within reach of one injected instruction, with no separate approval for the outbound step.

situations.title: An automated triage agent running on its builder's account
reach: Each new work item's summary and description, and its comments and attachments
Details from other work items on the site, used to build context
On a User's account (the default if no agent account is set up): every app, space and restricted page the person who built the automation can access
Write tools in the same step: update fields, create work items, post comments, and create, edit or delete content
Third-party tools authenticated as the user, such as sending Slack messages or Gmail email that appear to come from that person
Public web pages and web search, on by default unless an organisation admin turns them off
asked_our_example: Read each new work item and post a triage suggestion (fields, duplicates, links) as a comment
Work only in this one Jira space
Send no messages or email outside the team
gap: On a User's account the automated agent can reach and act on everything its builder can, including restricted spaces, and in automations no human approves each action.
Text anyone can type into a work item becomes agent input, and Atlassian says guardrail instructions are suggestions with no guarantee the agent will follow them.
Third-party tools act as the user once authenticated, and web access is on by default.

situations.title: A third-party MCP agent takes Atlassian data out
reach: Atlassian data the user sends into the agent, which may be passed to the vendor's MCP server
The vendor system itself: CRM data and sales workflows in HubSpot, documents in Box
Code generated and run in Replit through a Beta MCP server
Content returned from the third-party source into Atlassian, including modalities Atlassian does not control
asked_our_example: Look up customer context in the CRM for a Jira epic
Write no Atlassian content into third-party systems
gap: Data that leaves through a third-party MCP server is not covered by the Atlassian Customer Agreement commitments or Privacy Policy while in that environment, and Atlassian does not guarantee the server's security.

questions: PromptArmor reported in August 2026 that Rovo's URL-retrieval tool would open a URL the agent had composed, even with web search off: has that path been closed, and does the newer Web access toggle now govern every outbound request an agent makes, including Markdown images?

Your docs disagree on automated agents: one page says an agent in an automation cannot use its own tools, another that it can perform write actions directly. Which is current, and does an agent attached to a Jira workflow transition or board column ask anyone before it writes?
Can an organisation admin require every automated agent to run on its own agent account, so that no automation falls back to the builder's account and permissions?
Can a customer see, per agent run, every URL fetched and every piece of Atlassian content sent to a third-party MCP server, and export that record?
Guardrail instructions are described as suggestions: is there any enforced, non-prompt control that marks uploaded files, work item text or web content as untrusted before an agent can act on it?
incidents: 2026-08-05: PromptArmor published an indirect prompt-injection chain in which a file uploaded to Rovo made it send Jira tickets and Confluence documents to an attacker's URL through its URL-retrieval tool, with web search switched off. Disclosed to Atlassian on 23 May 2026; PromptArmor said it was unresolved when published. Its status after that date is unconfirmed in the sources read. [s31, s34, s35]

2026-07-08: RovoBlast (Varonis Threat Labs): a crafted link using the rovoChatPrompt parameter seeded attacker instructions into a signed-in user's Rovo Chat, and the ResearchAgent capability carried Confluence, Jira and SharePoint data out. Atlassian fixed it server-side on 8 July 2026, before the research was presented at DEF CON 34. [s32, s33, s34, s35]
As at 21 August 2026: Neither technique had a CVE, and neither research team reported exploitation against a live customer environment. [s35, s34]

help.pitch: RiskMandate would measure, for one real deployment of Atlassian's agents, what each agent was asked to do (its mandate), what its credentials and connections actually let it reach (its grant), and the difference between the two (the gap), and keep that as a written record. It is read-only: never in the request path.
